I am here tonight to talk about the gaps in the history curriculum regarding Asian history, specifically the exclusion of Imperial Japan's colonization and World War II war crimes. From 1894 to 1945, Imperial Japan invaded and colonized the Asia Pacific region, resulting in approximately 19 to 30 million deaths through multiple massacres, forced labor, starvation, military campaigns, and more.

These events affected multiple nations all over Asia, including China, Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines, Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand, and many, many more. The Rape of Nanking is one of these events in which over only six weeks Japan killed approximately 300,000 Chinese civilians and committed mass torture and destruction.

My own grandparents experienced these intense, forceful cultural suppression when Japan colonized Korea and saw their relatives and friends be sent off to war labor camps. Currently, the FCPS High School History course, World History and Geography II, has no formal criteria for teaching these events.

There are requirements to teach World War II events like D-Day, which are absolutely important to teach, but the events in Asia that affected people on a very similar scale are omitted. Asian American students make up about 19% of all FCPS students, and our history deserves to be valued.

History is about belonging. The lack of representation of this history that has such a massive impact on Asian students, countries, cultures, and families creates the opportunity to dismiss us as important and perpetuate stereotypes that Asians are outsiders whose struggles aren't worth being recognized.

In conclusion, I encourage the board to consider my proposal of the formal inclusion of these events in the history curriculum and to submit a formal request to the Virginia Department of Education in order to create a more inclusive and enriched history learning experience that makes FCPS students of all backgrounds feel seen and appreciated.
